name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q01 - Temperature conversion from Celsius to Fahrenheit

questiontext.text: A clinical thermometer records a body temperature of \(40.0^\circ\text{C}\). What is this temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conversion Formula
The relation between Fahrenheit temperature \(t_F\) and Celsius temperature \(t_C\) is given by \(t_F = \frac{9}{5}t_C + 32\).

Step 2: Substitution
Substituting \(t_C = 40.0^\circ\text{C}\): \(t_F = \frac{9}{5}(40.0) + 32\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(t_F = 9 \times 8.0 + 32 = 72.0 + 32 = 104.0^\circ\text{F}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature on the Fahrenheit scale is \(104.0^\circ\text{F}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q02 - Temperature rise equivalence in Fahrenheit

questiontext.text: During an experiment, the temperature of a liquid sample rises by \(30^\circ\text{C}\). What is this temperature rise on the Fahrenheit scale?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Temperature Interval Relation
A temperature interval of \(100\) Celsius degrees corresponds to \(180\) Fahrenheit degrees, giving \(\Delta t_F = \frac{9}{5}\Delta t_C\).

Step 2: Substitution
Given \(\Delta t_C = 30^\circ\text{C}\), \(\Delta t_F = \frac{9}{5}(30)\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(\Delta t_F = 9 \times 6 = 54^\circ\text{F}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature rise on the Fahrenheit scale is \(54^\circ\text{F}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q03 - Absolute temperature conversion to Celsius

questiontext.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at \(77.35\text{ K}\) under standard atmospheric pressure. What is its boiling point on the Celsius scale?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conversion Formula
The relationship between Celsius temperature \(t_C\) and Kelvin temperature \(T\) is \(t_C = T - 273.15\).

Step 2: Substitution
Substituting \(T = 77.35\text{ K}\): \(t_C = 77.35 - 273.15\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(t_C = -195.80^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The boiling point on the Celsius scale is \(-195.80^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q04 - Heat required to raise temperature of water

questiontext.text: How much heat energy is required to raise the temperature of \(2.0\text{ kg}\) of water from \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to \(75^\circ\text{C}\)? (Specific heat capacity of water \(= 4186\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula for Heat Absorbed
The heat required is given by \(Q = m s_w \Delta T\).

Step 2: Data Values
Mass \(m = 2.0\text{ kg}\), \(s_w = 4186\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), and \(\Delta T = 75 - 25 = 50^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(Q = 2.0 \times 4186 \times 50 = 100 \times 4186 = 4.186 \times 10^5\text{ J} = 418.6\text{ kJ}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The heat energy required is \(4.186 \times 10^5\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q05 - Heat required to melt a block of ice

questiontext.text: How much heat energy is needed to completely melt \(5.0\text{ kg}\) of ice at its normal melting point of \(0^\circ\text{C}\)? (Latent heat of fusion of water \(L_f = 3.33 \times 10^5\text{ J kg}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Latent Heat Formula
The heat required for a phase transition at constant temperature is \(Q = m L_f\).

Step 2: Data Substitution
Given \(m = 5.0\text{ kg}\) and \(L_f = 3.33 \times 10^5\text{ J kg}^{-1}\): \(Q = 5.0 \times 3.33 \times 10^5\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(Q = 16.65 \times 10^5\text{ J} = 1.665 \times 10^6\text{ J}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The heat required to melt the ice is \(1.665 \times 10^6\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q06 - Linear thermal expansion of an aluminium rod

questiontext.text: An aluminium rod has a length of \(2.0\text{ m}\) at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). What is the increase in its length when heated to \(120^\circ\text{C}\)? (Coefficient of linear expansion of aluminium \(\alpha = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Linear Expansion Formula
The increase in length is given by \(\Delta l = l_0 \alpha \Delta T\).

Step 2: Data Values
\(l_0 = 2.0\text{ m}\), \(\alpha = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\), and \(\Delta T = 120 - 20 = 100^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(\Delta l = 2.0 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \times 100 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 5.0\text{ mm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The increase in length is \(5.0\text{ mm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q07 - Radiant power comparison for different temperatures

questiontext.text: A spherical blackbody of radius \(R\) at absolute temperature \(300\text{ K}\) radiates power \(P_0\). What power will it radiate if its absolute temperature is raised to \(600\text{ K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
The total radiant power emitted by a blackbody is given by \(P = \sigma A T^4\).

Step 2: Temperature Ratio
Here the temperature increases by a factor of \(\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{600}{300} = 2\).

Step 3: Power Ratio Calculation
Since area remains constant, \(\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4 = 2^4 = 16\). Thus, \(P_2 = 16 P_0\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The radiated power will be \(16 P_0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q08 - Conversion of neon triple point to Celsius scale

questiontext.text: The triple point of neon is \(24.57\text{ K}\). Express this temperature on the Celsius scale.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conversion Formula
The relation connecting Kelvin temperature \(T\) and Celsius temperature \(t_C\) is \(t_C = T - 273.15\).

Step 2: Data Substitution
Given \(T = 24.57\text{ K}\), \(t_C = 24.57 - 273.15\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(t_C = -248.58^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The triple point of neon on the Celsius scale is \(-248.58^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q09 - Conversion of CO2 triple point to Fahrenheit scale

questiontext.text: The triple point of carbon dioxide is \(216.55\text{ K}\). Express this temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Celsius Conversion
First determine the Celsius temperature: \(t_C = T - 273.15 = 216.55 - 273.15 = -56.60^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 2: Fahrenheit Conversion Formula
\(t_F = \frac{9}{5}t_C + 32\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(t_F = \frac{9}{5}(-56.60) + 32 = -101.88 + 32 = -69.88^\circ\text{F}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The triple point of carbon dioxide on the Fahrenheit scale is \(-69.88^\circ\text{F}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q10 - Proportionality constant between absolute scales A and B

questiontext.text: Two absolute temperature scales \(A\) and \(B\) have the triple point of water defined to be \(200\text{ A}\) and \(350\text{ B}\), respectively. What is the reading on scale \(A\) when scale \(B\) reads \(140\text{ B}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Absolute Scale Relation
Since both scales are defined relative to absolute zero, temperatures are proportional to their defined triple points: \(\frac{T_A}{T_{A,\text{tr}}} = \frac{T_B}{T_{B,\text{tr}}}\).

Step 2: Substitution
Given \(T_{A,\text{tr}} = 200\text{ A}\) and \(T_{B,\text{tr}} = 350\text{ B}\), \(\frac{T_A}{200} = \frac{T_B}{350} \implies T_A = \frac{4}{7} T_B\).

Step 3: Calculation
For \(T_B = 140\text{ B}\): \(T_A = \frac{4}{7}(140) = 4 \times 20 = 80\text{ A}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The reading on scale A is \(80\text{ A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q11 - Temperature measurement with platinum resistance thermometer

questiontext.text: The resistance of a thermometer varies linearly with temperature. It has a resistance of \(101.6\ \Omega\) at the triple point of water (\(273.16\text{ K}\)) and \(165.5\ \Omega\) at the normal melting point of lead (\(600.50\text{ K}\)). What is the temperature when the resistance is \(123.4\ \Omega\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Linear Interpolation Formula
For a linear resistance variation, \(\frac{T - T_1}{T_2 - T_1} = \frac{R - R_1}{R_2 - R_1}\).

Step 2: Data Values
\(T_1 = 273.16\text{ K}\), \(R_1 = 101.6\ \Omega\), \(T_2 = 600.50\text{ K}\), \(R_2 = 165.5\ \Omega\), and \(R = 123.4\ \Omega\).

Step 3: Difference Calculations
\(R_2 - R_1 = 165.5 - 101.6 = 63.9\ \Omega\); \(R - R_1 = 123.4 - 101.6 = 21.8\ \Omega\); \(T_2 - T_1 = 600.50 - 273.16 = 327.34\text{ K}\).

Step 4: Solving for Temperature
\(T = 273.16 + 327.34 \times \frac{21.8}{63.9} = 273.16 + 111.67 = 384.83\text{ K} \approx 384.8\text{ K}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature corresponding to \(123.4\ \Omega\) is \(384.8\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q12 - Melting point of sulphur using constant volume thermometer

questiontext.text: In a constant-volume gas thermometer, the pressure of a sample of gas is \(1.250 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}\) at the triple point of water (\(273.16\text{ K}\)) and \(1.797 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}\) at the normal melting point of sulphur. What is the absolute temperature of the melting point of sulphur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Constant-Volume Law
At constant volume for an ideal gas, \(\frac{T}{T_{\text{tr}}} = \frac{P}{P_{\text{tr}}}\).

Step 2: Substitution
\(T = 273.16 \times \frac{1.797 \times 10^5}{1.250 \times 10^5} = 273.16 \times 1.4376\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(T \approx 392.7\text{ K}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The absolute temperature of the melting point of sulphur is \(392.7\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q13 - Actual length of rod measured by expanded steel tape

questiontext.text: A steel measuring tape calibrated at \(27.0^\circ\text{C}\) reads \(63.0\text{ cm}\) for the length of a rod on a hot day at \(45.0^\circ\text{C}\). Given \(\alpha_{\text{steel}} = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\), what is the actual length of the rod on that day?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Thermal Expansion of Tape
At \(45.0^\circ\text{C}\), each centimetre division expands by \(\Delta T = 45.0 - 27.0 = 18.0^\circ\text{C}\): \(1\text{ division} = 1 \times (1 + \alpha \Delta T)\text{ cm}\).

Step 2: Actual Length Formulation
\(L = 63.0 \times [1 + (1.20 \times 10^{-5} \times 18.0)] = 63.0 \times [1 + 2.16 \times 10^{-4}]\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(L = 63.0 + (63.0 \times 2.16 \times 10^{-4}) = 63.0 + 0.0136\text{ cm} = 63.0136\text{ cm} \approx 63.014\text{ cm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The actual length of the rod on that day is \(63.014\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q14 - Change in diameter of hole drilled in copper sheet

questiontext.text: A circular hole drilled in a copper plate has a diameter of \(4.24\text{ cm}\) at \(27.0^\circ\text{C}\). What is the increase in diameter when the plate is heated to \(227.0^\circ\text{C}\)? (\(\alpha_{\text{copper}} = 1.70 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cavity Expansion Principle
Any hole or cavity inside a solid expands at the exact same rate as the surrounding solid material: \(\Delta d = d_0 \alpha \Delta T\).

Step 2: Data Values
\(d_0 = 4.24\text{ cm}\), \(\alpha = 1.70 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\), and \(\Delta T = 227.0 - 27.0 = 200.0^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(\Delta d = 4.24 \times 1.70 \times 10^{-5} \times 200 = 4.24 \times 3.40 \times 10^{-3} = 1.4416 \times 10^{-2}\text{ cm} \approx 1.44 \times 10^{-2}\text{ cm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The increase in diameter of the hole is \(1.44 \times 10^{-2}\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q15 - Temperature needed to fit iron ring on wooden wheel rim

questiontext.text: An iron ring has an internal diameter of \(5.231\text{ m}\) at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). To fit tightly onto a wooden wheel rim of diameter \(5.243\text{ m}\), it must be expanded by heating. Given \(\alpha_{\text{iron}} = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\), to what temperature must the iron ring be heated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Expansion Requirement
The required change in diameter is \(\Delta D = 5.243 - 5.231 = 0.012\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Formula for Temperature Change
\(\Delta T = \frac{\Delta D}{D_0 \alpha} = \frac{0.012}{5.231 \times 1.20 \times 10^{-5}}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(\Delta T = \frac{0.012}{6.2772 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 191.16^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 4: Final Temperature
\(T = 27^\circ\text{C} + 191.2^\circ\text{C} \approx 218^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The iron ring must be heated to \(218^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q16 - Fractional change in liquid density due to heating

questiontext.text: The coefficient of volume expansion of glycerine is \(49 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\). What is the fractional decrease in its density when its temperature rises by \(30^\circ\text{C}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Density-Volume Relation
Mass is conserved, so \(\rho V = \rho' V'\). As volume expands, \(V' = V(1 + \alpha_v \Delta T)\), giving \(\rho' = \frac{\rho}{1 + \alpha_v \Delta T} \approx \rho(1 - \alpha_v \Delta T)\).

Step 2: Fractional Change Formulation
The fractional decrease in density is \(\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \approx \alpha_v \Delta T\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = 49 \times 10^{-5} \times 30 = 1.47 \times 10^{-2}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The fractional decrease in density is \(1.47 \times 10^{-2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q17 - Specific heat capacity calculation from calorimeter data

questiontext.text: An aluminium sphere of mass \(0.047\text{ kg}\) at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) is placed in a \(0.14\text{ kg}\) copper calorimeter containing \(0.25\text{ kg}\) of water at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). The mixture reaches a final steady temperature of \(23^\circ\text{C}\). Taking \(s_w = 4.18 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(s_{\text{Cu}} = 0.386 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), what is the specific heat capacity of aluminium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heat Lost by Aluminium
\(Q_{\text{lost}} = m_{\text{Al}} s_{\text{Al}} (100 - 23) = 0.047 \times 77 \times s_{\text{Al}} = 3.619 s_{\text{Al}}\).

Step 2: Heat Gained by Water and Calorimeter
\(Q_{\text{gained}} = (m_w s_w + m_{\text{Cu}} s_{\text{Cu}}) \times (23 - 20) = (0.25 \times 4180 + 0.14 \times 386) \times 3 = (1045 + 54.04) \times 3 = 1099.04 \times 3 = 3297.12\text{ J}\).

Step 3: Equating and Solving
\(3.619 s_{\text{Al}} = 3297.12 \implies s_{\text{Al}} = \frac{3297.12}{3.619} \approx 911\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 0.911\text{ kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The specific heat capacity of aluminium is \(0.911\text{ kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q18 - Calorimetric determination of latent heat of fusion of ice

questiontext.text: When \(0.15\text{ kg}\) of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) is mixed with \(0.30\text{ kg}\) of water at \(50.0^\circ\text{C}\), the final equilibrium temperature of the mixture is \(6.7^\circ\text{C}\). Given \(s_w = 4186\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), what is the latent heat of fusion of ice?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heat Lost by Warm Water
\(Q_{\text{lost}} = m_w s_w (50.0 - 6.7) = 0.30 \times 4186 \times 43.3 = 54376.14\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Heat Gained by Ice
Ice melts and warms: \(Q_{\text{gained}} = m_{\text{ice}} L_f + m_{\text{ice}} s_w (6.7 - 0) = 0.15 L_f + (0.15 \times 4186 \times 6.7) = 0.15 L_f + 4206.93\text{ J}\).

Step 3: Equating Heat Lost and Gained
\(0.15 L_f = 54376.14 - 4206.93 = 50169.21\text{ J}\).

Step 4: Solving for L_f
\(L_f = \frac{50169.21}{0.15} \approx 3.34 \times 10^5\text{ J kg}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The latent heat of fusion of ice is \(3.34 \times 10^5\text{ J kg}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q19 - Junction temperature in compound steel-copper rod

questiontext.text: A steel rod of length \(15.0\text{ cm}\) and cross-sectional area \(2A\) is joined to a copper rod of length \(10.0\text{ cm}\) and cross-sectional area \(A\). The steel end is at \(300^\circ\text{C}\) and the copper end is at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). Given \(K_{\text{steel}} = 50.2\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(K_{\text{Cu}} = 385\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), what is the steady-state junction temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heat Current Equality
Under steady-state conditions, heat current through the steel rod equals that through the copper rod: \(\frac{K_1 A_1 (300 - T)}{L_1} = \frac{K_2 A_2 (T - 0)}{L_2}\).

Step 2: Substitution
Substituting \(A_1 = 2A\), \(A_2 = A\), \(L_1 = 15\text{ cm}\), \(L_2 = 10\text{ cm}\): \(\frac{50.2 \times 2A (300 - T)}{15} = \frac{385 A T}{10}\).

Step 3: Simplification
\(\frac{100.4}{15}(300 - T) = 38.5 T \implies 6.6933(300 - T) = 38.5 T\).

Step 4: Solving for T
\(2008 - 6.6933 T = 38.5 T \implies 45.193 T = 2008 \implies T \approx 44.4^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The junction temperature in steady state is \(44.4^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q20 - Equivalent thermal conductivity of two identical joined bars

questiontext.text: An iron bar and a brass bar, both of identical length \(0.1\text{ m}\) and cross-sectional area \(0.02\text{ m}^2\), are soldered end to end. If their thermal conductivities are \(K_1 = 79\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(K_2 = 109\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), what is the equivalent thermal conductivity of the compound bar?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Harmonic Mean Formula
For two bars of equal dimensions in series, the equivalent thermal conductivity is the harmonic mean: \(K' = \frac{2K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2}\).

Step 2: Data Substitution
\(K' = \frac{2 \times 79 \times 109}{79 + 109} = \frac{17222}{188}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(K' \approx 91.6\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The equivalent thermal conductivity of the compound bar is \(91.6\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q21 - Radiant power emitted by a tungsten filament lamp

questiontext.text: A tungsten lamp filament operates at an absolute temperature of \(3000\text{ K}\) and has a total surface area of \(0.30\text{ cm}^2\). If the emissivity of tungsten at this temperature is \(0.40\) and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant is \(\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}\), what is the rate of radiant heat emission?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Stefan-Boltzmann Formula
The rate of heat emission is \(H = e \sigma A T^4\).

Step 2: Area Conversion
\(A = 0.30\text{ cm}^2 = 0.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^2\).

Step 3: Temperature Fourth Power
\(T^4 = (3000)^4 = (3 \times 10^3)^4 = 81 \times 10^{12}\text{ K}^4\).

Step 4: Calculation
\(H = 0.40 \times (5.67 \times 10^{-8}) \times (3.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times (81 \times 10^{12}) = 0.40 \times 5.67 \times 3.0 \times 81 \times 10^{-1} = 55.11 \approx 60\text{ W}\) (using \(0.3\text{ cm}^2\) and textbook rounding \(= 60\text{ W}\) or precisely \(55.1\text{ W}\)).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The rate of radiant heat emission is approximately \(55.1\text{ W}\) (or about \(60\text{ W}\) under typical rounded parameters).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q22 - Surface temperature of the Moon using Wien's law

questiontext.text: The spectral distribution of radiation from the surface of the Moon shows a peak wavelength at \(\lambda_m = 14.5\ \mu\text{m}\). Taking Wien's displacement constant as \(b = 2.90 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m K}\), what is the estimated surface temperature of the Moon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Wien's Displacement Law
\(\lambda_m T = b \implies T = \frac{b}{\lambda_m}\).

Step 2: Unit Conversion
\(\lambda_m = 14.5\ \mu\text{m} = 14.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(T = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m K}}{14.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}} = \frac{2900}{14.5} = 200\text{ K}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The estimated surface temperature of the Moon is \(200\text{ K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q23 - Cooling time calculation using Newton's law

questiontext.text: A bowl of soup cools from \(94^\circ\text{C}\) to \(86^\circ\text{C}\) in \(2.0\text{ minutes}\) in a room at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). How long will it take to cool from \(71^\circ\text{C}\) to \(69^\circ\text{C}\) under the same ambient conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Newton's Law Rate Equation
Rate of cooling: \(\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = K(T_{\text{avg}} - T_s)\).

Step 2: First Interval
Drop \(\Delta T_1 = 94 - 86 = 8^\circ\text{C}\) in \(2\text{ min}\); \(T_{\text{avg}, 1} = \frac{94 + 86}{2} = 90^\circ\text{C}\). Excess \(= 90 - 20 = 70^\circ\text{C}\). Thus, \(\frac{8}{2} = K(70) \implies 4 = 70 K\).

Step 3: Second Interval
Drop \(\Delta T_2 = 71 - 69 = 2^\circ\text{C}\) in time \(t_2\); \(T_{\text{avg}, 2} = \frac{71 + 69}{2} = 70^\circ\text{C}\). Excess \(= 70 - 20 = 50^\circ\text{C}\). Thus, \(\frac{2}{t_2} = K(50)\).

Step 4: Dividing Equations
\(\frac{4}{2 / t_2} = \frac{70}{50} \implies 2 t_2 = 1.4 \implies t_2 = 0.7\text{ min} = 42\text{ s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The time taken to cool from \(71^\circ\text{C}\) to \(69^\circ\text{C}\) is \(42\text{ seconds}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q24 - Radiative heat loss rate of human skin

questiontext.text: A person with a skin surface area of \(1.9\text{ m}^2\) and skin temperature of \(28^\circ\text{C}\) (\(301\text{ K}\)) stands in a room at \(22^\circ\text{C}\) (\(295\text{ K}\)). If the emissivity of the skin is \(0.97\) and \(\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}\), what is the net rate of radiant heat loss from the body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Net Radiant Heat Formula
\(H = e \sigma A (T^4 - T_s^4)\).

Step 2: Numerical Values
\(e = 0.97\), \(A = 1.9\text{ m}^2\), \(T = 301\text{ K}\), \(T_s = 295\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Fourth Power Difference
\(301^4 \approx 8.196 \times 10^9\text{ K}^4\); \(295^4 \approx 7.574 \times 10^9\text{ K}^4\). Difference \(= 0.622 \times 10^9\text{ K}^4\).

Step 4: Calculation
\(H = 0.97 \times (5.67 \times 10^{-8}) \times 1.9 \times (0.622 \times 10^9) \approx 66.4\text{ W}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The net rate of radiant heat loss is approximately \(66.4\text{ W}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q25 - Triple point of water on absolute scale with Fahrenheit interval size

questiontext.text: On an absolute temperature scale whose unit interval size equals that of the Fahrenheit scale (known as the Rankine scale), what is the absolute temperature of the triple point of water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Unit Size Comparison
One Kelvin degree corresponds to \(\frac{9}{5}\) Fahrenheit degree intervals.

Step 2: Absolute Scale Definition
On an absolute scale with interval size \(\Delta T = \frac{5}{9}\text{ K}\), absolute zero is \(0\). The triple point of water on the Kelvin scale is \(273.16\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Scale Conversion
Therefore, on this absolute scale: \(T = 273.16 \times \frac{9}{5} = 491.688\text{ units} \approx 491.69\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature of the triple point of water is approximately \(491.69\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q26 - Thermal stress developed in a rigidly clamped steel rail

questiontext.text: A continuous steel rail of cross-sectional area \(40\text{ cm}^2\) is laid at \(15^\circ\text{C}\) and rigidly clamped at its ends. On a hot summer day, its temperature rises to \(25^\circ\text{C}\). Given \(\alpha_{\text{steel}} = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\) and Young's modulus \(Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ N m}^{-2}\), what is the compressive force developed in the rail?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Thermal Strain
Since expansion is prevented, compressive strain is \(\frac{\Delta l}{l} = \alpha \Delta T = 1.20 \times 10^{-5} \times (25 - 15) = 1.20 \times 10^{-4}\).

Step 2: Thermal Stress
Stress \(\sigma = Y \left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\right) = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \times 1.20 \times 10^{-4} = 2.4 \times 10^7\text{ N m}^{-2}\).

Step 3: Compressive Force
Area \(A = 40\text{ cm}^2 = 40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2\). Force \(F = \sigma A = 2.4 \times 10^7 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 9.6 \times 10^4\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The compressive force developed in the rail is \(9.6 \times 10^4\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q27 - Tension developed in clamped brass wire upon cooling

questiontext.text: A brass wire of diameter \(2.0\text{ mm}\) is clamped taut between two rigid supports at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). If the temperature drops to \(-39^\circ\text{C}\), what is the tension developed in the wire? (Given \(\alpha = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\) and \(Y = 0.91 \times 10^{11}\text{ Pa}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Temperature Difference
\(\Delta T = 27 - (-39) = 66^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 2: Cross-Sectional Area
Radius \(r = 1.0\text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\). Area \(A = \pi r^2 = 3.1416 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2\).

Step 3: Thermal Stress
\(\sigma = Y \alpha \Delta T = 0.91 \times 10^{11} \times (2.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times 66 = 1.2012 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}\).

Step 4: Tension Calculation
\(F = \sigma A = 1.2012 \times 10^8 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-6} \approx 3.77 \times 10^2\text{ N} \approx 3.8 \times 10^2\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The tension developed in the wire is approximately \(3.8 \times 10^2\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q28 - Combined expansion of joined brass and steel rods

questiontext.text: A brass rod of length \(50\text{ cm}\) is joined end to end to a steel rod of length \(50\text{ cm}\), both having diameter \(3.0\text{ mm}\). The original lengths are at \(40.0^\circ\text{C}\). If the ends are completely free to expand, what is the change in total length of the combined rod at \(250.0^\circ\text{C}\)? (\(\alpha_{\text{brass}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\), \(\alpha_{\text{steel}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Temperature Rise
\(\Delta T = 250.0 - 40.0 = 210.0^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 2: Expansion of Brass
\(\Delta l_1 = l_1 \alpha_1 \Delta T = 50\text{ cm} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 210 = 0.210\text{ cm}\).

Step 3: Expansion of Steel
\(\Delta l_2 = l_2 \alpha_2 \Delta T = 50\text{ cm} \times 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 210 = 0.126\text{ cm}\).

Step 4: Total Expansion
\(\Delta l_{\text{total}} = \Delta l_1 + \Delta l_2 = 0.210 + 0.126 = 0.336\text{ cm} \approx 0.34\text{ cm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The total increase in length is \(0.34\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q29 - Heat required to convert subzero ice to steam

questiontext.text: What is the total heat required to convert \(3.0\text{ kg}\) of ice at \(-12.0^\circ\text{C}\) to steam at \(100.0^\circ\text{C}\) at standard atmospheric pressure? (Given: \(s_{\text{ice}} = 2100\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), \(L_f = 3.35 \times 10^5\text{ J kg}^{-1}\), \(s_w = 4186\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), \(L_v = 2.256 \times 10^6\text{ J kg}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Step 1: Heating Ice to 0 C
\(Q_1 = m s_{\text{ice}} \Delta T_1 = 3.0 \times 2100 \times 12.0 = 75600\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Step 2: Melting Ice
\(Q_2 = m L_f = 3.0 \times (3.35 \times 10^5) = 1005000\text{ J}\).

Step 3: Step 3: Heating Water to 100 C
\(Q_3 = m s_w \Delta T_2 = 3.0 \times 4186 \times 100.0 = 1255800\text{ J}\).

Step 4: Step 4: Vaporising Water
\(Q_4 = m L_v = 3.0 \times (2.256 \times 10^6) = 6768000\text{ J}\).

Step 5: Step 5: Total Heat
\(Q_{\text{total}} = 75600 + 1005000 + 1255800 + 6768000 = 9.1044 \times 10^6\text{ J} \approx 9.1 \times 10^6\text{ J}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The total heat required is \(9.1 \times 10^6\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q30 - Temperature rise of aluminium block under boring machine

questiontext.text: A \(10\text{ kW}\) drilling machine bores an \(8.0\text{ kg}\) aluminium block for \(2.5\text{ minutes}\). If \(50\%\) of the power is lost to the surroundings or used to heat the machine, what is the temperature rise of the aluminium block? (Specific heat capacity of aluminium \(= 0.91\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 910\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Total Work Done
Power \(P = 10\text{ kW} = 10^4\text{ W}\). Time \(t = 2.5 \times 60 = 150\text{ s}\). Total energy \(W = 10^4 \times 150 = 1.5 \times 10^6\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Heat Absorbed by Block
Effective heat delivered \(Q = 0.50 \times 1.5 \times 10^6 = 7.5 \times 10^5\text{ J}\).

Step 3: Temperature Rise Equation
\(Q = m s \Delta T \implies \Delta T = \frac{7.5 \times 10^5}{8.0 \times 910} = \frac{750000}{7280} \approx 103^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature rise of the aluminium block is approximately \(103^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q31 - Mass of ice melted by a red-hot copper block

questiontext.text: A \(2.5\text{ kg}\) copper block at \(500^\circ\text{C}\) is placed on a large block of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). What is the maximum mass of ice that can melt? (Specific heat of copper \(= 0.39\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), latent heat of fusion of water \(= 335\text{ J g}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heat Released by Copper Block
The copper cools from \(500^\circ\text{C}\) to \(0^\circ\text{C}\): \(Q = m_{\text{Cu}} s_{\text{Cu}} \Delta T = 2500\text{ g} \times 0.39\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 500\text{ K} = 487500\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Mass of Melted Ice Formula
\(Q = m_{\text{ice}} L_f\).

Step 3: Calculation
\(m_{\text{ice}} = \frac{487500\text{ J}}{335\text{ J g}^{-1}} \approx 1455\text{ g} \approx 1.5\text{ kg}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The maximum mass of ice that can melt is approximately \(1.5\text{ kg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q32 - Rate of sweat evaporation to reduce fever in child

questiontext.text: A child of mass \(30\text{ kg}\) running a fever of \(101^\circ\text{F}\) is given an antipyretic drug that lowers the fever to \(98^\circ\text{F}\) in \(20\text{ minutes}\). Assuming heat is lost solely by extra evaporation of sweat, specific heat of human body equals that of water (\(1.0\text{ cal g}^{-1}{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)), and latent heat of evaporation of water is \(580\text{ cal g}^{-1}\), what is the average rate of extra sweat evaporation in \(\text{g/min}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Temperature Drop in Celsius
\(\Delta t_F = 101 - 98 = 3^\circ\text{F}\). In Celsius, \(\Delta t_C = \frac{5}{9}(3) = \frac{5}{3}^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 2: Heat Lost by Body
Mass \(m = 30\text{ kg} = 30000\text{ g}\). \(Q = m s \Delta t_C = 30000 \times 1.0 \times \frac{5}{3} = 50000\text{ cal}\).

Step 3: Mass of Evaporated Sweat
\(m_{\text{sweat}} = \frac{Q}{L_v} = \frac{50000\text{ cal}}{580\text{ cal g}^{-1}} \approx 86.2\text{ g}\).

Step 4: Rate of Evaporation
Time \(= 20\text{ min}\). Evaporation rate \(= \frac{86.2\text{ g}}{20\text{ min}} \approx 4.31\text{ g/min} \approx 4.3\text{ g/min}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The average rate of extra sweat evaporation is approximately \(4.3\text{ g/min}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q33 - Mass of ice remaining in insulated cubical box

questiontext.text: A cubical thermacole icebox of outer side \(30\text{ cm}\) has walls of thickness \(5.0\text{ cm}\). It contains \(4.0\text{ kg}\) of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). The ambient temperature is \(45^\circ\text{C}\). If thermal conductivity of thermacole is \(0.01\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and latent heat of fusion of water is \(335 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\), what mass of ice remains after \(6.0\text{ hours}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Surface Area of Cube
Total area of \(6\) faces: \(A = 6 \times (0.30\text{ m})^2 = 6 \times 0.09 = 0.54\text{ m}^2\).

Step 2: Conduction Rate
Thickness \(L = 0.05\text{ m}\), \(\Delta T = 45 - 0 = 45^\circ\text{C}\). Heat current \(H = \frac{K A \Delta T}{L} = \frac{0.01 \times 0.54 \times 45}{0.05} = 4.86\text{ W}\).

Step 3: Total Heat in 6 Hours
Time \(t = 6 \times 3600 = 21600\text{ s}\). Total heat \(Q = 4.86 \times 21600 = 104976\text{ J}\).

Step 4: Melted and Remaining Mass
Melted mass \(m_{\text{melt}} = \frac{104976}{335 \times 10^3} \approx 0.313\text{ kg}\). Remaining ice \(= 4.0 - 0.313 = 3.687\text{ kg} \approx 3.7\text{ kg}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The mass of ice remaining after 6 hours is approximately \(3.7\text{ kg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q34 - Flame temperature under brass boiler boiling water

questiontext.text: A brass boiler has a base area of \(0.15\text{ m}^2\) and thickness \(1.0\text{ cm}\). It boils water at the rate of \(6.0\text{ kg/min}\) at atmospheric pressure (\(100^\circ\text{C}\)). If thermal conductivity of brass is \(109\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and latent heat of vaporisation of water is \(2256 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\), what is the temperature of the boiler surface in contact with the flame?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Heat Current Requirement
Boiling rate \(\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{6.0\text{ kg}}{60\text{ s}} = 0.10\text{ kg/s}\). Heat current \(H = 0.10 \times (2256 \times 10^3) = 2.256 \times 10^5\text{ W}\).

Step 2: Conduction Formula
\(H = \frac{K A (T_{\text{flame}} - 100)}{L} \implies T_{\text{flame}} - 100 = \frac{H L}{K A}\).

Step 3: Data Substitution
\(T_{\text{flame}} - 100 = \frac{2.256 \times 10^5 \times 0.01}{109 \times 0.15} = \frac{2256}{16.35} \approx 137.98^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 4: Final Flame Temperature
\(T_{\text{flame}} = 100 + 138 = 238^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The temperature of the boiler surface in contact with the flame is approximately \(238^\circ\text{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q35 - Newton's cooling law over consecutive temperature ranges

questiontext.text: A body cools from \(80^\circ\text{C}\) to \(50^\circ\text{C}\) in \(5.0\text{ minutes}\) in surroundings at \(20^\circ\text{C}\). How long will it take to cool from \(60^\circ\text{C}\) to \(30^\circ\text{C}\) in the same surroundings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: First Interval Analysis
Temperature drop \(\Delta T_1 = 80 - 50 = 30^\circ\text{C}\) in \(5\text{ min}\). Mean temperature \(T_{\text{avg}, 1} = \frac{80 + 50}{2} = 65^\circ\text{C}\). Excess temperature \(= 65 - 20 = 45^\circ\text{C}\). Rate: \(\frac{30}{5} = K(45) \implies 6 = 45 K \implies K = \frac{2}{15}\text{ min}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Second Interval Analysis
Temperature drop \(\Delta T_2 = 60 - 30 = 30^\circ\text{C}\) in time \(t\). Mean temperature \(T_{\text{avg}, 2} = \frac{60 + 30}{2} = 45^\circ\text{C}\). Excess temperature \(= 45 - 20 = 25^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 3: Rate Formulation
\(\frac{30}{t} = K(25) = \left(\frac{2}{15}\right) \times 25 = \frac{10}{3}\).

Step 4: Solving for Time
\(t = \frac{30 \times 3}{10} = 9.0\text{ minutes}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The time required to cool from \(60^\circ\text{C}\) to \(30^\circ\text{C}\) is \(9.0\text{ minutes}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMAL_PROPERTIES_OF_MATTER_MCQ_Q36 - Temperature needed to fit steel shaft into wheel hub using dry ice

questiontext.text: A steel wheel has a central hole of diameter \(8.69\text{ cm}\) at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). A steel shaft has an outer diameter of \(8.70\text{ cm}\) at the same temperature. To what temperature must the shaft be cooled using dry ice so that the wheel slips onto it? (\(\alpha_{\text{steel}} = 1.20 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Required Contraction
Change in diameter \(\Delta D = 8.69 - 8.70 = -0.01\text{ cm}\).

Step 2: Contraction Equation
\(\Delta D = D_0 \alpha \Delta T \implies \Delta T = \frac{-0.01}{8.70 \times 1.20 \times 10^{-5}}\).

Step 3: Temperature Change Calculation
\(\Delta T = \frac{-0.01}{1.044 \times 10^{-4}} \approx -95.78^\circ\text{C} \approx -95.8^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 4: Final Temperature
\(T = 27^\circ\text{C} + (-95.8^\circ\text{C}) = -68.8^\circ\text{C} \approx -69^\circ\text{C}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The shaft must be cooled to approximately \(-69^\circ\text{C}\).
